1037.title: Tibet, 1950–1959
1037.hook: Chinese forces entered Tibet; the Dalai Lama left for India, and others followed him into exile
1037.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep their practice in rebuilt monasteries, schools and community centers, and some hold Tibet and all who suffered in their daily prayers and loving-kindness practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Myanmar: monks who walked for their people, and monks who stood against hatred spoken in the robe's name. Your line: the robe for peace. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

What would you carry if you had to leave home at night, on foot, over mountains, not knowing when you'd come back? A coat. Water. A photograph, maybe. Some Tibetan families who crossed into India and Nepal speak of carrying something else too: a text wrapped in cloth, a small image of the Buddha, prayer beads, a teacher walking a few steps ahead. Today isn't one night. It's a long exile, and the practice that went with it.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?` → `A TEXT WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `A LONG EXILE.`

segments.voice: In the years named in today's title, Chinese forces entered Tibet, and Tibet came under the government in Beijing. The Chinese government and Tibetans in exile tell those years very differently, and this lesson won't settle that argument. What it can tell is what happened to a community of practice. After unrest in Lhasa, the Dalai Lama, whom Tibetan Buddhists hold as a great teacher, left for India. Monks, nuns and lay families followed through the high passes. In India, with very little, they rebuilt. Monasteries with the old names rose again, so a monastery from Tibet might now stand in the hot plains of southern India. Schools taught children their language and their texts. Debate courtyards filled again with monks clapping as they argued a point, just as their teachers had. And in his public teaching from exile, the Dalai Lama has returned again and again to compassion, even for those he disagrees with. An opponent, he has said, can be your teacher of patience. The Pali word is khanti, and the Dhammapada sets it very high. In Max Müller's translation: "The Awakened call patience the highest penance." Patience here doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. Exile still hurts; homes are still missed. Patience lets a person keep the grief without letting it harden into hate, and keep teaching while they wait.

segments.voice: Hold refugees in metta, loving-kindness: bring to mind anyone who has had to leave home, Tibetan families, refugees from anywhere, someone you know, and with each out-breath send a simple wish in words that feel true, may you be safe, may you find a home. If the mind drifts to the news or to blame, come back to the wish. Last, widen it to everyone caught up in that history, on every side.
Tibet. The high land whose teachers and families carried their practice into exile, and rebuilt it, monastery by monastery, far from home. Today's word.
Your line: the long exile. Grief kept, and the teaching kept, while they wait. Day one thousand thirty-seven, done.

1038.title: Cambodia's killing years
1038.hook: the Khmer Rouge closed the monasteries and killed monks; the sangha was rebuilt from very few
1038.howItsDone: Cambodian Buddhists remember those years at ceremonies for the dead and at the monasteries that were rebuilt, and monks and lay people have kept up walks and gatherings for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tibet, and families who walked into exile and rebuilt their monasteries far from home. Your line: the long exile. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

A monk can't ordain himself. In the Theravada tradition, a new monk is received by a gathering of monks already ordained, chanting together, so the robe passes hand to hand in an unbroken line. Usually that line is so ordinary nobody thinks about it. Then comes a time when the gathering itself almost disappears. What happens to a tradition when there are hardly enough monks left to make a new one?
screen: `A MONK CAN'T ORDAIN HIMSELF.` → `THE GATHERING RECEIVES HIM.` → `WHAT IF IT VANISHES?`

segments.voice: In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge took power and set out to remake the whole country from nothing. Cities were emptied. Money, schools and markets were abolished. Religion was treated as an enemy. Monasteries were closed or turned into prisons and storehouses. Monks were forced out of their robes, sent to labor in the fields, and killed. Old palm-leaf texts were burned or left to rot. It is hard to say how much was lost. When the regime fell, the sangha, the community of monks, had to be rebuilt from the few who were left: monks who had survived by hiding, or in exile, or by putting the robe aside. Ordinations began again. Monasteries reopened, sometimes in buildings that still bore the marks of what had been done there. One monk who survived abroad, Maha Ghosananda, came home and led peace walks across the country, monks, nuns and lay people side by side through places still scarred by war. He taught that peace is made the way a walk is made, step by step, and each step can be a meditation. After those years, that was not a pleasant gesture. It was a hard choice about what to rebuild. And it shows this: a line of practice can come close to breaking and still continue. The gathering grew again, one ordination at a time, until there were monks enough to receive the next.

1039.title: Saigon, 1963
1039.hook: the monk Thich Quang Duc died in protest against the persecution of Buddhists; told with care, never as an example
1039.howItsDone: Vietnamese Buddhist communities remember Thich Quang Duc at memorial services, and some teachers who speak of him frame his death within the protest's call to end suffering, not as something to imitate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cambodia, and a sangha rebuilt one upasampada, one ordination, at a time. Your line: rebuilt from few. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

Before anything else today, a word about how this story is told. It involves a death, and it is a hard story. It's told here so that you know it, not so that anyone copies it. If you are carrying thoughts of harming yourself today, please pause this lesson and reach out to someone near you, or to a local crisis line. You matter more than any lesson. Now, a city street, and a protest that the world saw.
screen: `A HARD STORY, TOLD WITH CARE.` → `NOT AN EXAMPLE.` → `IF YOU'RE HURTING, REACH OUT.`

segments.voice: In South Vietnam, Buddhists were protesting against the government of the day. They said they were treated unfairly: limits on flying the Buddhist flag, arrests, and violence against those who gathered. Monks and nuns marched, fasted and held vigils. Then, at a busy crossroads in Saigon, a monk named Thich Quang Duc sat down in the meditation posture and ended his own life, as a protest. A photograph of that moment went around the world, and the pressure on the government grew. Here is where care matters. Buddhist teachers have not agreed about how to understand what he did. The first precept of Buddhist ethics is to abstain from taking life, and some teachers include one's own life in that. Some have described his act as a self-offering, made out of compassion, to draw the world's eyes to suffering. Others have said that, whatever his intention, it should never be repeated, and have mourned it as a loss. Both kinds of voices honor the man; they read his death differently. What the accounts share is the suffering around it: people afraid to practice their faith openly, and a protest meant to make the world look. So the lesson isn't the act. It's the suffering that came before it, and the monks, nuns and lay people who kept protesting with marches, fasts and vigils. To tell this story with care is to keep both in view: the courage people saw, and the life that ended.
screen: `BUDDHISTS PROTEST UNFAIR TREATMENT.` · `A MONK'S PROTEST AT A CROSSROADS.` · `TEACHERS READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `KEEP THE SUFFERING IN VIEW.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your chest, if that's comfortable, and feel it rise and fall. Bring to mind the people in this story, those afraid to gather, the monk, the people who watched, the families, and let compassion, karuna, touch it the way you'd hold something fragile; you don't have to understand everything. If it feels heavy, come back to the hand on your chest and the breath beneath it.

Your line: told with care. Gentle is enough, for a story this heavy. That's day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Mongolia's monasteries
1040.hook: monasteries were torn down and monks killed; years later, practice returned
1040.howItsDone: Mongolian Buddhists visit rebuilt monasteries to make offerings, light butter lamps and ask monks for blessings, and some families still keep images and texts their relatives once hid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saigon, a hard story about protest and loss. Your line: told with care. Day one thousand forty.

On the open grasslands of Mongolia, in some places only foundations show in the grass: a line of stones, a raised floor, a scatter of broken tile. Herders ride past them. Some of those stones were once monasteries, with chanting halls and young monks learning their texts. How does a monastery disappear? And how, years later, does practice come back to a place that had almost forgotten it?
screen: `STONES IN THE GRASS.` → `ONCE A MONASTERY.` → `HOW DOES PRACTICE COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Buddhism had long been woven into Mongolian life, in the Tibetan form of the tradition, with monasteries large and small across the country. Then, under a communist government closely tied to the Soviet Union, a campaign turned against it. Monasteries were torn down or emptied. Monks were arrested and killed, or forced to return to lay life and marry. Statues were melted; texts were burned. Yet some things were hidden. Families buried images in the ground or kept a text at the back of a chest. Some former monks kept the chants in their heads, saying them quietly at home. When the government changed, the doors opened again. Old monks who still remembered the ceremonies taught young ones. Monasteries were rebuilt, sometimes on the old foundations, and people came back to make offerings and ask for blessings. The return wasn't neat. Teachers had to be found, texts recovered, a whole way of training started again almost from memory. But it happened. The Dhammapada has a pair of verses for those quiet years. Someone who recites a great deal of the teaching but doesn't live it is like a cowherd counting other people's cows. Someone who recites only a little, but lives it, letting go of greed, hatred and delusion, has a real share in the renunciant's life. An old monk in a back room, saying a few remembered lines under his breath, was not counting anyone's cows. A little, kept and lived, was enough to start again.
screen: `A CAMPAIGN AGAINST THE MONASTERIES.` · `IMAGES BURIED, CHANTS REMEMBERED.` · `OLD MONKS TEACH YOUNG ONES.` · then, large: `A LITTLE, KEPT AND LIVED.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on the breath at the belly, and when the mind wanders off, to a plan, a worry, a song, notice it: that moment of noticing is a small return, the same shape as a chant remembered after long silence. Say silently, back, and begin again with the next breath. Don't count the returns or judge them; let each one be welcome.
Mongolia's monasteries. Torn down in a campaign against religion, remembered in hidden texts and quiet chants, and rebuilt when the doors opened again. Today's word.

1041.title: China's Cultural Revolution
1041.hook: temples were closed and monks sent away; since then, the doors have reopened
1041.howItsDone: In reopened temples in China, lay Buddhists offer incense, bow before the Buddha images and join chanting services, and monks and nuns again train novices under the rules that now govern religious life there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mongolia's monasteries: buried images, remembered chants, and old monks teaching young ones. Your line: it returned. Day one thousand forty-one.

A temple door is heavy, often painted red, with rows of round studs and a high wooden threshold you step over rather than on. In the mornings a monk swings it open; in the evenings it closes. For a stretch of years in China, temple doors stayed shut, some with a chain across them. Today, what happened behind those doors, and the morning they began to open again.
screen: `A HEAVY RED DOOR.` → `SHUT, WITH A CHAIN.` → `THE MORNING IT OPENED.`

segments.voice: The Cultural Revolution was a political campaign in China, launched by Mao Zedong, to sweep away what it called old ideas, old customs, old culture and old habits. Other religions came under attack too, not Buddhism alone. Young Red Guards entered temples, smashed statues and burned scriptures. Temples were closed, or turned into factories, schools and storehouses. Monks and nuns were sent away to labor or made to return to lay life, and some were beaten or killed. For years, practicing openly could be dangerous. People who lived through it tell of a statue walled up behind plaster, and the Buddha's name said under the breath at home. When the campaign ended and policy changed, temples began to reopen. Statues were repaired or carved again. Some monks who had survived, gray now, returned to their old monasteries and trained new novices. Religious life in China today still runs under government rules, and people inside and outside the country describe those rules very differently. But the doors did reopen, and there are temples busy again with incense and chanting. The Dhammapada has a verse for those who kept steady. In Max Müller's translation: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." The campaign was a great wind of blame. Some people, quietly, did not falter, and the temples stand open now partly because of what they kept.
screen: `A CAMPAIGN AGAINST THE OLD.` · `TEMPLES CLOSED, STATUES SMASHED.` · `HIDDEN BEHIND PLASTER.` · then, large: `A SOLID ROCK IN THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Picture a reopened temple: the heavy door swinging open, your foot stepping over the threshold, incense in the air, a bell somewhere inside and the low sound of chanting. Notice the people, an old woman lighting incense, a monk sweeping, a family with a child, and let yourself simply be glad the door is open. When the mind wanders, come back to the doorway and step through again.

1042.title: Bamiyan remembered
1042.hook: the empty niches in the cliff where the great Buddhas stood
1042.howItsDone: Buddhists and others remember Bamiyan in talks, exhibitions and visits to the valley, and the question of whether to rebuild the statues or leave the niches empty is still discussed among scholars, local people and heritage bodies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, China's Cultural Revolution, and the sì, the temple doors, chained shut and then swung open. Your line: the doors reopened. Day one thousand forty-two.

A tall arch is cut deep into a honey-colored cliff. It's the shape of a standing figure, but there's no figure in it. Just rock, scarred and hollow, with small caves around it where people once lived and prayed. Farther along the cliff, another arch, another emptiness. Below, fields and poplar trees, and children walking to school. The cliff is in Afghanistan, in the valley of Bamiyan. Today we sit with what used to stand there.
screen: `AN ARCH IN THE CLIFF.` → `NO FIGURE IN IT.` → `THE VALLEY OF BAMIYAN.`

segments.voice: Long ago, great standing Buddhas were carved into that cliff, looking out over a valley on old trade routes. Monks lived in the caves around them, and travelers and pilgrims passed through and wrote about what they saw. Long after the valley's people had become Muslim, the statues stayed, part of the landscape and of local memory. Then the Taliban government of the time declared them idols and destroyed them with explosives. People from around the world and from different faiths, Muslims among them, spoke out against it. What was left were the empty niches. Since then, a long debate. Some want to rebuild the Buddhas. Some say the niches should stay empty, as a witness to what happened. Once, an image of a Buddha was projected into a niche in light. Bamiyan raises a sharp Buddhist question: what is lost when a statue is lost? Images of the Buddha are deeply honored; people bow, offer flowers, and some speak of feeling the Buddha near. Yet the old texts tell of a monk named Vakkali, sick and near death, who longed to look at the Buddha's body one more time. At his bedside, the Buddha asked what good it would do to see this decaying body: whoever sees the teaching sees him, and whoever sees him sees the teaching. So the niches can be read two ways at once. They are a real loss, and grief for them makes sense. And what the statues pointed to, the teaching, did not fall with the stone.
screen: `GREAT BUDDHAS IN THE CLIFF.` · `DESTROYED, LEAVING EMPTY NICHES.` · `REBUILD, OR LEAVE THEM EMPTY?` · then, large: `THE TEACHING DID NOT FALL.`

segments.voice: Rest your eyes on an empty space near you, an empty chair, a doorway, the space between your hands, or close them and feel the quiet room around you. Notice the urge to fill it with a thought, a plan, a song, and let the urge pass; if something you've lost comes to mind, let it sit there with you a while. The emptiness can hold grief and calm at once.
Bamiyan remembered. The valley in Afghanistan where great Buddhas stood in the cliff, and where the empty niches still remind people of what was there. Today's word.
Your line: the empty niches. The stone fell, but the teaching didn't fall with it. See you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Images are deeply honored, so grief makes sense. But Vakkali was told whoever sees the teaching sees the Buddha, and the teaching didn't fall.

1043.title: Conversion and caste
1043.hook: the Ambedkarite movement today, and Buddhism as a path of dignity in India
1043.howItsDone: Ambedkarite Buddhists gather at neighborhood viharas and community halls, take the refuges and precepts together, read Ambedkar's writings in study circles, greet one another with "Jai Bhim", and some return each year to the ground in Nagpur where he took refuge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bamiyan, and two empty niches in a cliff. Your line: the empty niches. Day one thousand forty-three, the end of a hard week.

"Jai Bhim." In parts of India, that's how some Buddhists greet each other: victory to Bhim. Bhim is Bhimrao Ambedkar, and his portrait hangs beside the Buddha's in some homes and community halls, and on banners at gatherings. He wears a suit and glasses and holds a book. Why does a lawyer in a suit sit next to the Buddha? Today's story is about birth, about dignity, and about a choice a whole movement made.
screen: `JAI BHIM.` → `A PORTRAIT BESIDE THE BUDDHA.` → `BIRTH AND DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: An old scene fits today. A brahmin tending his sacred fire sees the Buddha on his alms round and shouts at him to stop where he is, calling him an outcast. The Buddha doesn't defend his own family. He asks whether the man even knows what makes an outcast. Then he answers: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. Deeds make a person either. That is the Vasala Sutta, and the Dhammapada says much the same. As this path told some weeks ago, B. R. Ambedkar, born into a community treated as untouchable, took refuge in the Buddha with a great crowd in Nagpur. His followers carry that choice into ordinary places. Small viharas stand in city neighborhoods and villages, his portrait beside the Buddha's. Study circles read his book, The Buddha and His Dhamma. Some families take the refuges and precepts together at weddings and naming ceremonies. Each year, on the anniversary, crowds return to the ground in Nagpur. At gatherings you'll hear his call: educate, agitate, organize. For many in the movement, dignity means schooling, work and fair treatment as well as the refuges, and some describe Buddhism as the path that gave it all a name. People of other traditions in India, Hindus among them, have also worked against caste; this isn't a contest between faiths. It's the story of people told by birth that they were less, who now greet each other with two words: Jai Bhim. So a hard week ends: Tibet in exile, Cambodia rebuilt, Saigon told with care, Mongolia and China reopening, Bamiyan's empty niches, and a path chosen for dignity. Every day, something kept.
screen: `NOT BY BIRTH, BY DEEDS.` · `VIHARAS, STUDY CIRCLES, NAGPUR.` · `EDUCATE, AGITATE, ORGANIZE.` · then, large: `A PATH OF DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone people tend to overlook, the person who cleans the building, the one who collects the trash, a neighbor others talk past, and see their face if you can. With each in-breath, notice that they have a whole life, as full as yours; with each out-breath, wish them well.
Ambedkar. The movement he began, still alive in neighborhood viharas and study circles, where worth is measured by deeds, not by birth. Today's word.
Your line: a path of dignity. Worth is measured by deeds, not by birth. That's day one thousand forty-three.
